media.title: VSCO (photo app, launched 2011)
media.note: the aesthetic is named for the app's muted-filter look, though by 2019 it referred more to the fashion than the photo edit

reacts_against: the heavily posed, filtered 'Instagram baddie' look that preceded it; VSCO girl styling presented itself as effortless and environmentally conscious (metal straws, reusable bottles).
article: The VSCO girl look is unusual on this list because it names a photo filter rather than a garment, a scene or a decade. VSCO, a photo-editing app launched in 2011, built its identity on desaturated, slightly faded presets that made ordinary phone photos look like they'd been shot on film — muted greens, soft warm whites, no oversaturated reds. By 2019 "VSCO girl" had drifted from describing a photo style to describing the person who posted that way: oversized T-shirts, scrunchies worn three deep on one wrist, Birkenstocks, a Hydro Flask armored in stickers, and a studied, performed casualness that positioned itself against the heavily posed, contoured "Instagram baddie" look dominant just before it. The trend burned hot and fast on TikTok for a single summer, driven largely by parody videos ("and I oop—") as much as by genuine adopters, and faded almost as quickly as it arrived. Its color signature — sun-faded, slightly cool-toned, nothing fully saturated — is really the VSCO app's own filter math, which makes it one of the few aesthetics on this list whose palette can be traced to a specific piece of software rather than a subculture, a place or an era.
